extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and constitutional law; informed general readers interested in federalism
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of federal system and constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of the merits, operation, and development of a federal system and of constitutional change in the United States, including modes of change and practical consequences. Focuses on how federal and state powers interact and how constitutions evolve by amendment, interpretation, and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of machinery for local fiscal control and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: It provides the machinery for a better control of the taxes raised and expended in a given region of the country, and a better oversight of the public works undertaken there than would be possible were everything left to the Central government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the federal system enables regional (State) control over taxation and public works suited to local needs. Also notes a caveat about the educative effect of frequent elections: 'elections in America are too many and come too frequently... leave him at the mercy of knots of selfish adventurers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of State system for localizing disorders and experimenting
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility of the State system in localizing disorders or discontents, and the opportunities it affords for trying easily and safely experiments which ought to be tried in legislation and administration, constitute benefits to be set off against the risk ... that evils may continue in a district ... and invite imitation by other States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States serve as laboratories for legislation/administration, allowing experimentation on a smaller scale; but there is risk that local evils persist and spread — a trade-off to weigh when evaluating federal structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of legislative powers relieves central legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of the State legislatures relieves Congress of a burden too heavy for its shoulders; ... it could not possibly, were its competence as large as theirs, deal with the multiform and increasing demands of the different parts of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the practical necessity of dividing legislative functions because of regional diversity in conditions and needs; central legislature could not effectively craft measures suited to widely varying local circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: National authority and constitutional supremacy as stabilizing devices
rubrics_metrics.description: It has given the National government a direct authority over all citizens, irrespective of the State governments, and has therefore been able safely to leave wide powers in the hands of those governments. And by placing the Constitution above both the National and the State governments, it has referred the arbitrament of disputes between them to an independent body ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights two constitutional devices: (1) direct national authority over individuals enabling decentralized state powers, and (2) supremacy of the Constitution with an independent interpreter (the courts) which together promote stability and reverence for the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of political contrivances depends on adaptation to people
rubrics_metrics.description: The true value of a political contrivance resides not in its ingenuity but in its adaptation to the temper and circumstances of the people for whom it is designed, in its power of using, fostering, and giving a legal form to those forces of sentiment and interest which it finds in being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsels caution in transplanting institutions: an institutional device that succeeded in one country may fail in another if not suited to local sentiments, capacities, and habits (examples: slavery strained Federal fabric; love of Union strengthened it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid versus Flexible Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries the Constitution is changeable by the ordinary legislature (Flexible Constitution). In others the rules are placed above the legislature and changeable only by some superior authority (Rigid Constitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines both types and gives exemplars: the English Constitution as Flexible, the American as Rigid. Notes practical consequences: rigid constitutions resist legislative change but are not absolutely unchangeable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of constitutional development: Amendment, Interpretation, Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been changed by Amendment. ... It has been developed by Interpretation, that is, by the unfolding of the meaning implicitly contained in its necessarily brief terms. It has been developed by Usage, that is, by the establishment of rules not inconsistent with its express provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains relative strength and character of each mode: Amendment is direct and most effective but most difficult; Interpretation (chiefly by courts) is potent while it stands and effectively incorporated; Usage (practice, statutes, conventions) is easiest and most frequent but weakest and subordinate to the Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of framing proposed amendments (A and B)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) Congress may itself, by a two-thirds vote in each house, prepare and propose amendments. (B) The legislatures of two-thirds of the States may require Congress to summon a Constitutional Convention; the Convention when called shall draft and submit amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies there are two ways to propose amendments. Notes that when legislatures require a convention, Congress must call it and composition/election procedures of the convention are not specified in the Constitution (left to Congress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of ratifying amendments (X and Y) and historical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: (X) The legislatures of three-fourths of the States may ratify any amendments submitted to them. (Y) Conventions may be called in the several States, and three-fourths of these conventions may ratify. On all occasions the amending power has used method A for proposing and method X for ratifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes legal particulars: Congress may prescribe which ratification method; President's consent not required; two-thirds in Congress needed to bring certain measures; historically A+X used; omission: no time fixed for ratification, which is inconvenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single protected provision in amendment process (equal state suffrage)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is only one provision of the Constitution which cannot be changed by this process. It is that which secures to each and every State equal representation in one branch of the legislature. 'No State without its consent shall be deprived of its equal suffrage in the Senate' (Art. V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains this is not absolute unanimity among all States but grants any particular State an absolute veto over proposals that would deprive it of equal Senate representation; emphasizes limits to amendatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping and purposes of the existing amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendments made ... have been in all seventeen in number. They have been made on five occasions, and fall into five groups... The first group, including ten amendments ... constitute what the Americans ... call a Bill of Rights... The fourth group comprises three amendments (xiii., xiv., xv.) which forbid slavery, define citizenship, endeavour to secure the suffrage ... and extend Federal protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes substantive aims and historical context of amendment groups: Bill of Rights as supplement; later amendments as corrections or as results of crisis (e.g., Civil War) enacted under extraordinary conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general tendencies affecting the Federal system (Supplementary Note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three tendencies: (1) The importance of the things which the National Government does has tended to increase. (2) Uniformity of regulation over the country has become more needful. (3) In matters regulated partly by National Government and partly by the States, the inconvenience arising from division and intermingling of powers has become more evident and more serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples: larger army/navy, tariff affecting trade, conservation and waterways, need for uniform labor/safety/health laws, and railroad regulation; notes political reluctance to depart from existing federal/state boundaries despite growing pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of constitutional rigidity and inevitability of change
rubrics_metrics.description: No constitution can be made to stand unsusceptible of change, because if it were, it would cease to be suitable to the conditions amid which it has to work ... If we find a Rigid Constitution tenacious of life, we may be sure that it has not stood wholly changeless, but has been so modified as to have adapted itself to the always altering circumstances that have grown up round it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that even 'rigid' constitutions evolve (by amendment, interpretation, usage) to adapt to changing circumstances; predicts ongoing modification of the American Constitution though its words may remain largely the same.
